representative.title: Spectral Thermal Boundary Conductance Calibration via Phonon Spectroscopy Feedback in van der Waals Heterostructures
representative.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat dissipation in nanoscale devices are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet kinetic transport models rely on static boundary assumptions that fail to predict when interface resistance overtakes bulk resistance. We replace the static Kapitza resistance assumption with a dynamically calibrated spectral thermal boundary conductance, driven by iterative model-experiment calibration using mean-free-path-resolving phonon spectroscopy in dielectric-dielectric systems. By closing the loop between time-domain thermoreflectance measurements and the phonon Boltzmann transport equation via inverse modeling, we establish the exact physical and power-density thresholds where interfacial resistance dominates, explicitly decoupling phonon spectral mismatch from electron-phonon and defect-scattering confounders. This mechanism-commit innovation resolves the unmapped boundary variable gap, enabling predictive thermal design for high-power-density electronics.
representative.core_contribution: Replacing the static boundary assumption in kinetic transport models with a dynamically calibrated spectral thermal boundary conductance in dielectric-dielectric van der Waals heterostructures, iteratively refined via inverse modeling of phonon spectroscopy data to define the precise power-density threshold where interfacial thermal resistance overtakes bulk thermal resistance, while isolating the signal from electron-phonon and defect-scattering confounders.
representative.method:
Conceptual Move: Replace the static boundary assumption in kinetic transport modeling with a dynamic, closed-loop calibration driven by experimental phonon spectroscopy characterization.

Step 1 (Rewire phonon_spectroscopy_characterization -> interfacial_boundary_variable): Use time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) and frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) with variable modulation frequencies to measure phonon group velocities, mode-specific scattering rates, and spectral transmission at the van der Waals heterostructure interface. Feed these measurements into a bounded delta update rule that iteratively adjusts the spectral thermal boundary conductance (the interfacial_boundary_variable) in the phonon Boltzmann transport equation. Require corroboration across multiple spectral windows before updating Kapitza resistance parameters.

Step 2 (bulk_conduction_ablation protocol): Disable the interfacial feedback loop and assume bulk-dominated Fourier transport with a fixed, literature-value boundary condition. Compare the predicted total thermal resistance against the closed-loop calibrated model to isolate the contribution of the dynamically calibrated boundary variable to overall thermal resistance.

Step 3 (high_power_density_stress protocol): Subject the heterostructure to progressively increasing power densities while monitoring feedback loop convergence. Record the power-density threshold where non-equilibrium hot optical phonon populations cause the calibrated boundary variable to diverge, explicitly defining the model's validity boundary.
representative.risks:
Risk 1: Phonon spectroscopy (TDTR/FDTR) may suffer from spatial averaging that convolves bulk and interfacial scattering, corrupting the inverse modeling signal. Mitigation: Use frequency-domain thermoreflectance with variable modulation frequencies to selectively probe different thermal penetration depths, isolating the interfacial contribution from bulk phonon scattering.

Risk 2: High power density stress may induce non-linear phonon-phonon scattering (three-phonon Umklapp processes) that breaks the linear boundary conductance assumption. Mitigation: Explicitly bound the model's validity to the regime where hot optical phonon populations remain below the threshold for dominant non-equilibrium effects, and record this threshold as a measurable failure boundary.

Risk 3: Interfacial defects or impurities could mimic spectral mismatch. Mitigation: Restrict the material system to high-quality dielectric-dielectric van der Waals interfaces and use structural characterization (e.g., STEM) to bound the defect density, ensuring defect-scattering does not confound the phonon spectroscopy signal.

representative.title: Moiré Potential Landscapes Dictate the Thermal Cycling Stability of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Van Der Waals Heterostructures
representative.abstract: Engineered interlayer twist angles suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures, but their stability under operational thermal cycling remains unverified across diverse materials. We replace the complex shear-strain locking mechanism with a fundamental boundary condition governed by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape. We demonstrate that engineered twist angles remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the local moiré potential energy barriers, and in the absence of confounding defect-mediated or chemically-induced pinning. By synthesizing heterostructures across diverse material families and subjecting them to controlled thermal cycling, we isolate the moiré potential mechanism and establish the material-dependent limits of thermal anisotropy retention.
representative.core_contribution: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy under operational thermal cycling is strictly bounded by a critical interlayer binding energy threshold dictated by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape, specifically in regimes where defect-mediated and chemically-induced interlayer pinning are negligible.
representative.method: We conceptualize the stability of random interlayer rotations not through complex interlayer shear-strain locking feedback loops, but through the fundamental energy barriers of the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape. We synthesize a library of van der Waals heterostructures (e.g., MoS2/WS2, MoSe2/WSe2, graphene/hBN) with controlled random interlayer rotations. We subject these structures to sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients. We then characterize the cross-plane thermal conductivity before and after cycling. By comparing the thermal anisotropy retention across materials with varying moiré potential depths, we perform a material-dependent binding energy ablation to isolate the moiré potential mechanism and confirm the critical energy threshold for structural stability.
representative.risks: Primary risk is that thermal cycling could induce interlayer diffusion or chemical bonding (e.g., via chalcogen vacancies) that pins the layers, providing an alternative explanation for the retention of thermal anisotropy independent of moiré potential pinning. Mitigation involves using low-temperature cycling regimes and verifying structural integrity via cross-sectional TEM to rule out chemical bridging. Secondary risk is that thermal contact resistance changes during cycling could mimic changes in intrinsic cross-plane thermal conductivity. Mitigation involves using suspended membrane geometries and time-domain thermoreflectance to decouple contact resistance from intrinsic material properties.
representative.rationale: This skill application resolves the missing assumption of structural stability and the material generality boundary condition by replacing the parent's complex shear-strain locking mechanism with a fundamental, material-dependent moiré potential energy threshold. It sharpens the parent idea's thesis by grounding the operational stability of thermal anisotropy in a clear, falsifiable physical mechanism that naturally extends across diverse van der Waals material families.

representative.title: Flux-Dependent Spectral Transmission Threshold for the Bulk-to-Interface Thermal Resistance Crossover
representative.abstract: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance is traditionally modeled using static acoustic mismatch or equilibrium bonding energy thresholds. We propose a representation shift: defining the critical crossover boundary through the flux-dependent spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations. By modulating interface bonding energy and applying high-power-density heat flux, we demonstrate that the critical threshold shifts predictably as hot phonons alter the effective transmission probability via anharmonic interactions. This non-equilibrium spectral transmission model resolves the validity domain of the maximum transmission limit for weakly bonded interfaces and identifies the precise boundary variable governing the crossover under operational conditions, explicitly decoupled from local thermal expansion and equilibrium bulk scattering artifacts.
representative.core_contribution: The critical interface bonding energy threshold for the bulk-to-interface thermal resistance crossover is not a static material constant, but a flux-dependent parameter defined by the spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations, shifting the validity boundary of the maximum transmission limit under high power density independent of equilibrium thermal expansion.
representative.method: Conceptual move: Shift the representation of the interface boundary from a static acoustic mismatch threshold to a flux-dependent spectral transmission threshold. Methodology: 1) Synthesize phononic_interface_systems (e.g., Si/Ge heterostructures) with systematically varied interface_bonding_energy_modulation via controlled surface functionalization. 2) Rewire the experimental loop such that ultrafast_spectral_phonon_characterization directly informs iterative interface_bonding_energy_modulation to pinpoint the crossover boundary. 3) Perform isotopic_mean_free_path_ablation using isotopically pure vs. natural materials to decouple bulk phonon mean free path from interface scattering. 4) Apply high_power_density_heat_flux_stress to stress test the feedback loop, confirming the shifted boundary condition and recording failure boundaries where irreversible interface reconstruction occurs.
representative.risks: ['Risk 1: High-power-density measurements may induce local thermal expansion or irreversible interface reconstruction, masking the non-equilibrium phonon effect. Mitigation: Use ultrafast pulsed heating with low duty cycles and mechanically constrain the interface.', 'Risk 2: Isotopic ablation might introduce unintended interface defects. Mitigation: Rigorous TEM and XPS characterization.', 'Risk 3: The observed threshold shift may be conflated with bulk thermal conductivity changes. Mitigation: Use isotopic ablation to decouple bulk mean free path effects.']
representative.rationale: This representation shift resolves the unmapped boundary variable by explicitly defining the crossover threshold in terms of non-equilibrium phonon spectral overlap, rather than static bonding energy. It addresses the missing boundary condition by delineating the validity domain of the maximum transmission limit for non-ideal interfaces under high flux, directly repairing the parent idea's scope without altering its core thesis.

representative.title: Direct Observation of Saturating Interfacial Thermal Conductance in Annealed Graphene/SiO2 Heterostructures Reveals Bonding-Dependent Phonon Transmission Limits
representative.abstract: Interfacial thermal boundary resistance fundamentally limits heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing thermal conductance saturation remain unobserved. We demonstrate that interfacial thermal conductance in graphene/SiO2 heterostructures saturates at a critical covalent bond density, revealing a fundamental limit to phonon transmission enhancement through interface engineering. Using ultrafast thermoreflectance spectroscopy, we directly observe non-monotonic thermal conductance evolution during controlled annealing, where initial van der Waals-to-covalent bonding transitions increase conductance, but excessive covalent bonding introduces defect scattering that degrades heat transfer. This discriminating observation falsifies monotonic bonding-conductance models and establishes a bonding-configuration-dependent upper bound on interfacial thermal transport.
representative.core_contribution: Interfacial thermal conductance exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on covalent bond density, saturating and then degrading due to competing phonon transmission enhancement and defect scattering mechanisms, establishing a fundamental material-dependent limit on thermal transport across engineered interfaces.
representative.method: We synthesize graphene/SiO2 van der Waals heterostructures via chemical vapor deposition and dry transfer to create atomically sharp interfaces. We apply controlled thermal annealing (200-600°C in vacuum) to systematically tune interfacial bonding from pure van der Waals to mixed van der Waals-covalent to defect-rich covalent configurations. We characterize the atomic bonding configuration using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy to quantify covalent bond density (C-O-Si bridge bonds) and defect concentration. We measure interfacial thermal conductance using ultrafast thermoreflectance spectroscopy with <10 ps temporal resolution across the annealing series. We ablate the mechanism by comparing as-grown van der Waals interfaces, optimally annealed interfaces at peak conductance, and over-annealed defect-rich interfaces to isolate bonding configuration effects from bulk property changes, directly observing the saturation and degradation of thermal conductance.
representative.risks: Risk 1: Annealing may cause graphene degradation rather than controlled interface modification. Mitigation: Use Raman spectroscopy to monitor graphene quality (2D/G ratio) and limit annealing temperature to <600°C where graphene remains intact. Risk 2: Thermal conductance changes may be dominated by bulk SiO2 property changes rather than interface effects. Mitigation: Use thickness-controlled SiO2 samples (>100 nm) and compare with bulk SiO2 thermal conductivity measurements to isolate interface contribution. Risk 3: Ultrafast thermoreflectance may not achieve sufficient sensitivity for sub-nm interface layers. Mitigation: Use high-repetition-rate laser system (80 MHz) and lock-in detection with signal averaging to achieve <1% measurement uncertainty on thermal decay time constants.
representative.rationale: This skill application resolves the direct_observation gap by providing direct experimental observation of thermal conductance saturation at atomic-scale interfaces under controlled bonding configurations. The verification reversal route ensures the mechanism is back-inferred from observable thermal transport limits rather than assumed a priori. The non-monotonic conductance dependence serves as a pre-registered discriminating outcome that falsifies simple monotonic bonding-conductance models and establishes a fundamental upper bound on interfacial thermal transport.

representative.title: Commensurability-Mediated Covalent Phonon Bridging in van der Waals Heterostructures for High-Power-Density Thermal Dissipation
representative.abstract: The fundamental limit of heat transfer across van der Waals interfaces is conventionally attributed to weak interfacial coupling and diffuse phonon scattering. We invert this premise by demonstrating that covalent interfacial functionalization does not universally enhance thermal boundary conductance; rather, it acts as a commensurability-mediated phonon bridge. By precisely controlling the interfacial atomic registry via twist-angle alignment in graphene/hexagonal boron nitride heterostructures, we show that covalent functionalization yields a massive thermal boundary conductance spike only in commensurate (aligned) registries with minimized moiré strain, while acting as a scattering sink in incommensurate ones. Using time-domain thermoreflectance, we bound the maximum heat flux limits under high power density, revealing that atomic alignment dictates the efficacy of covalent thermal bridging, provided intralayer defect scattering is minimized and twist-angle-dependent electron-phonon coupling variations are decoupled.
representative.core_contribution: The thermal boundary conductance enhancement via covalent interfacial functionalization is strictly dependent on the interfacial atomic registry and minimized moiré strain, establishing commensurability as the fundamental structural invariant for overcoming van der Waals thermal bottlenecks, contingent on sub-percolation defect densities and decoupled from twist-angle-dependent electron-phonon coupling.
representative.method: The conceptual move replaces the assumption of universal weak van der Waals scattering with a commensurability-mediated covalent phonon bridging mechanism. We synthesize van der Waals heterostructures (graphene/hBN) with controlled twist angles (0° commensurate and 30° incommensurate) using deterministic dry transfer to tune the interfacial atomic registry. We then apply covalent interfacial functionalization via diazonium grafting at ultra-low density (<0.1% coverage) to modulate bonding strength while preserving intralayer transport. We characterize the thermal boundary conductance using time-domain thermoreflectance under high-power-density pumping (up to 10 GW/m²). We perform a twist-angle moiré ablation, comparing the thermal response of commensurate (0°) versus incommensurate (30°) registries to isolate the registry-dependent effect. Local Raman mapping and in situ Raman thermometry verify registry preservation and detect structural degradation thresholds.
representative.risks: ['1) Diazonium grafting may introduce excessive point defects in the graphene lattice, degrading intrinsic in-plane thermal conductivity and masking interfacial gains. Mitigation: use ultra-low-density functionalization (<0.1% coverage).', '2) High-power-density pumping in time-domain thermoreflectance may induce irreversible interfacial delamination. Mitigation: employ in situ Raman thermometry to detect structural degradation thresholds.', '3) The interfacial twist angle may relax or shift during chemical functionalization, inducing moiré strain. Mitigation: use deterministic dry transfer with edge-clamping and verify via Raman.', '4) Local structural relaxation around covalent bonds in incommensurate interfaces might create localized commensurate patches, artificially inflating the incommensurate thermal conductance. Mitigation: high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) to verify the absence of local relaxation.', '5) Twist-angle-dependent variations in electron-phonon coupling could confound the purely phononic bridging mechanism. Mitigation: utilize pump-probe techniques with varying excitation wavelengths to decouple electronic and phononic contributions.']
